title: Alkenes: electrophilic addition
source: Questions copied unchanged from the mission-lesson scripts for CCEA A-level Chemistry (status of the source: mission-lesson scripts of Oct-Nov 2026 (reviewed by AI reviewers; not signed off by a person)). Terms and clues: OR12#t2 term and clue written for the game; OR12#t1 term and clue written for the game; OR12#t3 term and clue written for the game; OR12#t4 term and clue written for the game. Questions: OR12#N.2, OR12#N.6, OR12#N.11, OR12#N.14, OR12#N.16.

assemble.prompt: Match each term to its definition.

items.label: Heterolytic fission
items.clue: A covalent bond breaks and both electrons go to one atom, forming two ions.

items.label: Electrophile
items.clue: A pair acceptor, such as H⁺ or the δ+ atom of a polar molecule, attracted to a C=C.

items.label: Carbocation
items.clue: A species containing C⁺ with only three bonds, formed after the C=C attacks Hδ+ or Brδ+.

items.label: Bromine water
items.clue: Orange test reagent that turns colourless when shaken with an alkene but stays orange with an alkane.

questions.stem: Which set contains only species that can act as electrophiles?

options.text: H⁺, NO₂⁺, OH⁻
Br₂, HBr, NH₃
H⁺, NO₂⁺, Br₂
NO₂⁺, H⁺, Cl⁻

questions.explanation: Each can accept an electron pair. H⁺ has no electrons, NO₂⁺ is positive and electron-deficient, and Br₂ accepts a pair from a C=C bond.

questions.stem: Ethene is bubbled through a solution of bromine in an organic solvent at room temperature, in the dark. Which statement is correct?

options.text: The bromine loses its colour as CH₂BrCH₂Br forms by addition.
The bromine loses its colour as CH₂=CHBr forms by substitution.
No reaction occurs, as Br₂ has no positive charge.
No reaction occurs, as UV light is needed to split Br₂.

questions.explanation: Br₂ adds across the C=C bond: CH₂=CH₂ + Br₂ → CH₂BrCH₂Br. The orange-brown colour of bromine disappears; this is the test for C=C.

questions.stem: 2,3-dimethylbut-2-ene, (CH₃)₂C=C(CH₃)₂, reacts with hydrogen bromide. What is the product?

options.text: (CH₃)₂CBr–CBr(CH₃)₂
(CH₃)₂C=C(CH₃)CH₂Br
(CH₃)₂CH–CH(CH₃)₂
(CH₃)₂CH–CBr(CH₃)₂

questions.explanation: HBr adds across C=C: H to one carbon, Br to the other. The double bond becomes single. Both carbons are alike, so there is one product, 2-bromo-2,3-dimethylbutane.

questions.stem: Ethene reacts with hydrogen bromide by electrophilic addition. Which describes the curly arrows in the first step of the mechanism?

options.text: From the H atom of HBr to the C=C bond, and from Br to the H–Br bond
From the C=C bond to the Br of HBr, and from the H–Br bond to the H
From the C=C bond to the H of HBr, and from the H–Br bond to Br
Fish-hook arrows split H–Br into H• and Br•, which add to C=C

questions.explanation: The electron-rich C=C bond donates a pair to the δ+ H atom, forming a C–H bond, while the H–Br bonding pair moves onto Br. This gives CH₃CH₂⁺ and Br⁻; Br⁻ then bonds to the carbocation.

questions.stem: In the dark, at room temperature, but-2-ene quickly decolourises a solution of iodine monochloride, ICl. Butane does not react with it. The product is CH₃CHICHClCH₃. Which statement explains why but-2-ene reacts without light?

options.text: The C=C bond is weaker than a C–C single bond, so it breaks easily without needing any light.
The electron-rich C=C donates a pair to Iδ+, and the I–Cl bond breaks heterolytically.
ICl splits into I• and Cl• radicals even in the dark, and these radicals attack only C=C bonds.
The carbon atoms of the C=C bond are electron-deficient, so they attract the Clδ− end of ICl.
